about: Thresholds the engine checks a schedule against. Each entry describes the shape of a rule and names the official source to read; none of it is legal advice. Coverage (which employers and workers a local rule applies to) is summarised in 'covers' and must be confirmed at the source. Premiums, notice periods and penalties are deliberately not recorded here: they change, and this file does not.

none.label: No local rule chosen (conservative default)
none.covers: Not a legal rule. A gap under 10 hours between a close and the next open is flagged because it is a fatigue and early-quit risk, wherever you are.

federal.label: US federal (FLSA)
federal.covers: Overtime after 40 hours in a workweek for non-exempt employees. Federal law sets no minimum rest between shifts; the 10-hour flag is the conservative default.

california.label: California (state)
california.covers: Daily overtime past 8 hours and double time past 12 hours in a workday for non-exempt employees, on top of weekly overtime; seventh-consecutive-day rules also apply and are not computed here. No statewide minimum rest between shifts.

oregon.label: Oregon predictive scheduling (statewide)
oregon.covers: Retail, hospitality and food service employers with 500 or more employees worldwide; workers whose duties relate to those operations.

seattle.label: Seattle Secure Scheduling
seattle.covers: Hourly employees of retail and food service businesses with 500 or more employees worldwide; full-service restaurants also need 40 or more full-service locations.

chicago.label: Chicago Fair Workweek
chicago.covers: Covered industries (including retail, restaurants, hotels, warehouses, healthcare, manufacturing, building services) above employer-size thresholds, for employees under an earnings ceiling the city updates each year.

evanston.label: Evanston Fair Workweek
evanston.covers: Hospitality, retail, warehouse, manufacturing and building services employers above employer-size thresholds; food service has its own thresholds.

nyc-fast-food.label: New York City Fair Workweek (fast food)
nyc-fast-food.covers: Fast food chains with 30 or more locations nationally. The retail part of the law has no rest rule.

nyc-retail.label: New York City Fair Workweek (retail)
nyc-retail.covers: Retail employers with 20 or more workers in New York City. No minimum rest rule; the 10-hour flag is the conservative default.

philadelphia.label: Philadelphia Fair Workweek
philadelphia.covers: Retail, hospitality and food service employers with 250 or more employees and 30 or more locations, including chains and franchises.

los-angeles-city.label: Los Angeles City Fair Work Week (retail)
los-angeles-city.covers: Retail employers with 300 or more employees globally, for work in the City of Los Angeles.

los-angeles-county.label: Los Angeles County Fair Workweek (unincorporated areas, retail)
los-angeles-county.covers: Retail employers with 300 or more employees globally, for work in unincorporated Los Angeles County.

berkeley.label: Berkeley Fair Workweek
berkeley.covers: Several industries, including retail, restaurants, hotels and warehouses, above local and global employer-size thresholds.

emeryville.label: Emeryville Fair Workweek
emeryville.covers: Retail and fast food employers above global or local employer-size thresholds.

san-francisco.label: San Francisco Formula Retail Employee Rights
san-francisco.covers: Formula retail with 40 or more locations worldwide and 20 or more employees in San Francisco. No minimum rest rule; the 10-hour flag is the conservative default.

sources_checked: Each official page above, as linked, on 2026-10-15; Oregon BOLI and Seattle Labor Standards read directly.
Cross-checked against two employer guides published in 2026 that summarise the same ordinances.
